description: AMB-039: escape sequences are prohibited in the unit value. Canonical form fixes one spelling per expression; JSON escapes would give that spelling many byte encodings, so the guarantee has to hold at the encoding layer too.

cases.rationale: Positive control. Every character legal in a unit string is legal unescaped in JSON, so the canonical form is always writable literally.

Decodes to MW, which is canonical — and that is exactly the problem. Accepting this makes the wire bytes something other than a function of the unit, so two producers tagging identical columns would emit different data digests (companion §5.2 step 3).

JSON permits an escaped solidus, so every unit string containing a division would otherwise have two legal encodings. This is the most likely one to appear by accident — several JSON writers escape / by default.
A third encoding of MW/h. Two escapes plus the literal form make three byte sequences for one canonical string; the prohibition collapses them to one.

An escaped backslash decodes to M\W, which is also a unit-grammar violation — but the metadata layer rejects it first. The layering matters: E_BAD_METADATA means "this is not how metadata is written", E_UNIT_SYNTAX means "this is not a unit".

A control character cannot be written literally in JSON, so an escape is the only way to smuggle one into a unit value. Prohibiting escapes closes the route entirely rather than enumerating forbidden code points.

An unpaired surrogate: valid JSON, and not valid UTF-8 once decoded. §5.2 requires the metadata blob to be UTF-8, so this is doubly wrong — and a reader that decodes before validating may produce a replacement character and carry on.

A byte-order mark written as a literal character, not an escape, so AMB-039 does not reach it. U+FEFF is outside the symbol class, making this a grammar violation rather than a metadata one — the two rules cover different halves of the same hazard.
